title: Exposing grammar myths and mistakes with Grammar Girl

entries.note: The guest's persona, begun as a podcast almost 20 years ago; linguists objected to the name because she mostly covers usage and punctuation, not strict [[see:grammar]].
Once a broad field of learning in Latin and Greek, later Latin and French learning in English, then narrowed to language and usage; shares a root with [[same-root:glamour]].
Its sense was extended to any kind of schooling, one stage in the shifting meaning of [[see:grammar]].
Comes from the same root as [[same-root:grammar]], which is why Roy Peter Clark called his book The Glamour of Grammar.
Also called the Oxford comma, the comma before the final 'and' in a list; a style choice, left out by AP style in simple lists and used by Chicago.
Traditionally used for uncountable things, but a singular-versus-plural rule covers the exceptions better, as in 'one less banana'; contrasted with [[see:fewer]].
Traditionally used for countable things, or under the Chicago rule for plurals; [[see:less]] in its place has been recorded since the 1500s.
A supermarket sign wording that Merriam-Webster calls idiomatic even though it breaks the [[see:fewer]] rule; [[see:Tesco]] replaced it with [[see:up to 10 items]].
Used for countable things, against [[see:much]] for uncountable ones; used to argue that groceries can be seen as a mass, so [[see:10 items or less]] works.
Used for uncountable things, against [[see:many]]; part of an argument in favour of [[see:10 items or less]].
A British supermarket chain criticised over its [[see:10 items or less]] sign, which it changed to [[see:up to 10 items]].
[[see:Tesco]]'s cop-out replacement for [[see:10 items or less]], which Rob says actually means nine.
Means fewer in number, unlike [[see:less bad people]]; a Guardian style guide example of where the [[see:fewer]] distinction matters.
Means people who are not as bad, unlike [[see:fewer bad people]].
Its figurative use bothers pedants, but Mark Twain, Dickens and F. Scott Fitzgerald used it that way, and Jane Austen mocked people who objected to it.
Readers said it only applies to two things, but the OED and a Samuel Johnson quote allow more, for a choice among distinct items; contrasted with [[see:among]].
Proposed by readers in place of [[see:between]] for three options; it suits a crowd better than a choice between distinct items.
A superlative Rob dislikes; Jess notes that '-ing' participles like [[see:excitingest]] rarely take the [[see:-est]] ending.
Acceptance of the superlative has lagged behind acceptance of [[see:fun]] as an adjective, so it still stands out more than [[see:most fun]].
Once only a noun; using it as an adjective ('a fun party') spread around the 1950s or 60s and still drew complaints 20 years ago.
Still objected to alongside [[see:funnest]], even though [[see:fun]] is now accepted as an adjective.
Draws less attention than [[see:funnest]] because people are now used to [[see:fun]] as an adjective.
A form nobody would use, cited to back up Rob's objection to [[see:winningest]].
A Germanic superlative suffix used on one-syllable adjectives, while words of three or more syllables take 'most'; Rob suggests the 'most' construction is a French habit.
French puts this word before an adjective to form a superlative, which Rob thinks English copied in its 'more/most' construction.
Itself a combination of a word meaning 'more' and the [[from:-est]] ending, in effect 'the morest'.
Given as an example of a Germanic word with the superlative ending, like [[see:most]].
A French-derived word that takes [[see:-est]], one counterexample to Rob's Germanic-versus-Romance theory.
Another non-Germanic word that takes [[see:-est]], weakening the Germanic-versus-Romance theory.
Required by the one-syllable rule, though the guest prefers 'more clear'.
An adjective used as an adverb, like [[see:slow]] or [[see:close]]; these are legitimate English and were once more common, as in 'violent hot' and 'horrid angry'.
A sign wording that pedants criticise but that is grammatical, because [[see:slow]] is a [[see:flat adverb]].
A [[see:flat adverb]] alongside the regular adverb 'slowly'; 'drive slow' and 'drive slowly' mean the same thing.
A [[see:flat adverb]] next to 'closely', used differently: 'stay close' but 'look closely'.
Another [[see:flat adverb]], as in 'drive fast'.
An old [[see:flat adverb]] use that shows they used to be more common.
Another old [[see:flat adverb]] use that has since dropped out.
For no known reason it isn't a [[see:flat adverb]], so 'swam badly' is correct; 'I feel bad' is about linking verbs instead.
The adverb ending is cognate with [[same-root:like]], so 'cleverly' is in effect 'clever like'; this is clearer in Dutch [[same-root:-lijk]].
Cognate with the adverb ending [[same-root:-ly]] in English and other Germanic languages.
A Dutch ending that sounds like 'like', making the link between [[same-root:-ly]] and [[same-root:like]] more obvious.
Word pairs that sound right only in one order; the tendencies are shorter, more powerful, more common, more positive, main or earlier item first.
One of the [[see:frozen binomials]]: the main part of the dish comes first, so 'cheese and macaroni' sounds wrong.
One of the [[see:frozen binomials]], with the shorter, more salient word first.
Shows the [[see:frozen binomials]] tendency to put the more powerful person, often the man, first.
An exception where the woman comes first, perhaps because the bride is the centre of attention at a wedding.
Shows the [[see:frozen binomials]] tendency to put the more common word first.

entries.term: put the cart before the horse
entries.note: Jokingly applied to reversing [[see:horse and carriage]]; Rob notes the idiom actually says cart.
Shows the more positive word coming first in [[see:frozen binomials]].
Like [[see:macaroni and cheese]], the main part of the meal comes first.
The British name for [[see:macaroni and cheese]], which drops the 'and' but keeps the same order.
Its order follows the order of events: you have to kiss before you can tell.
Follows the order of events but is famously flipped in the song [[see:Night and Day]].
A famous song that reverses the usual [[see:day and night]].
Gin is the main part of the drink so comes first; Billy Joel flips it to [[see:tonic and gin]] for the rhyme.
Billy Joel's reversal of [[see:gin and tonic]] in a song, done for the rhyme, which catches the ear.
The sound-order rule in pairs like [[see:tick-tock]]: I comes before A or O, so reversals like 'dong ding' sound deliberate.
Illustrates the vowel order of [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Never 'song-sing', an example of [[see:ablaut reduplication]] mixing a verb and a noun.
A verb pair among the [[see:frozen binomials]], ordered by events: you live before you learn.
Listed with other noun-only [[see:frozen binomials]].
A playful example of [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
A playful example of [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Shows I coming before O in [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Reversed as 'dong ding', it sounds deliberate, showing the [[see:ablaut reduplication]] order.
An example of [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Shows I before A in [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Shows I before A in [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Shows I before O in [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Shows I before A in [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
A memory aid for English adjective order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose; nobody really knows why the order feels right.
Age comes before origin under [[see:OSASCOMP]], so 'American young singer' sounds wrong.
Breaks [[see:OSASCOMP]], since 'bad' is an opinion, but fits [[see:ablaut reduplication]].
Another case where sound patterns override [[see:OSASCOMP]].
Can become 'square green tile' to single one out from a wall of green tiles, showing that breaking [[see:OSASCOMP]] can shift emphasis.
An example of normal [[see:OSASCOMP]] order.
German word-order rule for sentence information, contrasted with English flexibility to show how unusually strict [[see:OSASCOMP]] is.
Words that sound right together because they have been repeated together for so long, such as [[see:deeply regret]], which makes things harder for learners.
An example of [[see:collocation]].
An example of [[see:collocation]].
An example of [[see:collocation]].
A [[see:collocation]] meaning to spend time in prison; there is no necessary reason it uses 'do' rather than 'spend'.
A simple verb phrase given as an example of [[see:collocation]].
A simple verb phrase given as an example of [[see:collocation]].
Verb-plus-preposition combinations that learners find especially hard, so plain-language advice prefers one-word verbs, like [[see:surrender]] over [[see:give up]].
Means something very different from [[see:wipe out]], showing how [[see:phrasal verbs]] puzzle learners.
Contrasted with [[see:wipe up]] as an example of [[see:phrasal verbs]].
A phrasal verb that the one-word [[see:surrender]] can replace, unlike [[see:give out]] and [[see:give off]].
A one-word verb that is easier for learners than [[see:give up]].
Means something very different from [[see:give up]].
Also very different from [[see:give up]].
Age-related: people born after 1995 say it instead of [[see:by accident]]; Rob blames [[see:on purpose]], while the guest suspects a mass-media source like [[see:Barney]].
The form used by people born before 1970; [[see:on accident]] took over among younger, probably mainly American, speakers.
Rob thinks its 'on' was copied into [[see:on accident]]; the guest doubts this parallelism theory.
The children's show the guest jokingly blames, without proof, for the spread of [[see:on accident]].
Slangy internet use of 'because' straight before a noun; possibly from [[from?:because hey]] via [[see:Saturday Night Live]], first for silly reasons, now for any reason.
Its recurring 'hey, free dummy' sketch is thought to have started [[see:because hey]], and so [[see:because reasons]].
Shows the [[see:because reasons]] construction replacing 'because of my dog'.
A book by linguist Gretchen McCulloch on online language, its title using the [[see:because reasons]] construction.
From a [[see:Saturday Night Live]] sketch, as in 'because hey, free lemons'; dropping 'hey' supposedly gave [[gave?:because reasons]].
Turning nouns into verbs and vice versa, a long English tradition that Shakespeare used with [[see:ghosted]], [[see:portcullis]] and [[see:dog]].
Used by Shakespeare, an example of [[see:verbing]].
Mentioned alongside [[see:ghosted]] as a Shakespearean example of [[see:verbing]].
Used as a verb by Shakespeare, an example of [[see:verbing]].
Used as a verb by Shakespeare, an example of [[see:verbing]].
Making a verb from an existing noun, like [[see:evaluate]] from 'evaluation', or [[see:edit]] and [[see:babysit]].
Became an English word after 'evaluation', an example of [[see:back formation]].
Formed after 'regurgitation', an example of [[see:back formation]].
Formed after 'exploitation', an example of [[see:back formation]].
Formed after 'destruction', an example of [[see:back formation]].
Rob's favourite [[see:back formation]]: 'editor' came first, the verb later.
A [[see:back formation]] from 'babysitter', which existed first.
Rob dislikes it as a verb, a corporate-sounding example of [[see:verbing]].
Another verb use Rob resists, a corporate-sounding example of [[see:verbing]].
A kids' verb from 'versus', recorded since at least the 1980s, probably from gaming; it fills a gap, as in 'our school is versing them in a spelling bee'.
A TV show whose title was pronounced 'man verse food', the same clipping of 'versus' seen in [[see:versing]].
Kids also use the bare verb, as in 'I verse him', alongside [[see:versing]].
Gen Alpha slang roughly meaning doing something smart but dangerous, from [[from:yogurt]] split as [[from:yo, Gert]], with Gert becoming a meme character.
Reanalysed as [[see:yo, Gert]], the starting point of [[gave:gerting]].
[[from:yogurt]] turned into a sentence, creating the character Gert behind [[gave:gerting]].
